title: Brazil election: Lula wins fourth term in dramatic comeback over Bolsonaro
description: Figure caption, ByIone WellsReporting fromBrasília and Hafsa KhalilBrazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office in a d
body: Figure caption, ByIone WellsReporting fromBrasília and Hafsa KhalilBrazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office in a dramatic comeback over his right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro.Left-wing leader Lula took 51.79% of votes, becoming the first president since Brazil's return to civilian rule in 1985 to be elected after losing the first round of voting.Lula told jubilant crowds his victory was a "loss for negativity, lies", adding "long live democracy".Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, has so far refused to recognise the result and called for it to be annulled. World leaders have congratulated Lula on his re-election.Bolsonaro's rejection comes as no surprise to observers. His father did the same. But a challenge appears unlikely to succeed.Firstly, it seems to centre on the unprecedented decision by the Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin to extend voting nationwide by two hours. Some Bolsonaro fans are pointing out that Zanin was once Lula's lawyer and alleging bias.But both teams had requested an extension to voting times - Lula's had argued that voters in São Paulo and Bahia could not get to the polling stations because of a lack of buses, while Bolsonaro's campaign cited heavy rain in some areas in the south of the country and in São Paulo as their reason.Both knew every vote would count and did not want their side to  miss out.The president of the Supreme Electoral Court Kássio Nunes Marques –  appointed by Jair Bolsonaro – confirmed Lula's victory and said that the voter extension did not change the outcome of the race.The sheer gap between the two candidates' tallies -  4.4 million votes - makes the result more difficult  to challenge.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Lula is making history as the first Brazilian to be elected four timesThe result came as a surprise after Flávio Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October with 47% of votes ahead of Lula's 45%.But Lula's camp gained momentum ahead of election day, focusing on boosting voter turnout after 33 million people did not vote in round one. Sunday saw the largest drop in abstention between the two rounds of a presidential election since 1989.Bolsonaro had been poised to give a victory speech and said the result should be annulled, calling it "inexplicable".As his disconsolate supporters left the house in Brasília where their candidate had been watching the result, Lula took to the streets in São Paulo to celebrate."This, my fourth term, will be the best of any president in the history of this country," the former metal worker told supporters. "It will be the one in which I listen most to the Brazilian people."After pulling off this victory, Lula faces big hurdles: a divided country, an opponent that won't recognise the result, and a hostile Congress packed full of Bolsonaro allies.Markets reacted negatively to the unexpected outcome. The Sao Paolo stock exchange opened 15% down, sparking a brief suspension before recovering slightly. Interest rate futures rose as investors scrutinised Lula's fiscal plans.Reacting to the result, US President Donald Trump suggested the election had been stolen."I didn't take sides, but it looked like another rigged election," he told reporters on Monday, without providing evidence or more details. "It looked very bad to me."Other world leaders from across the political spectrum have congratulated Lula. Mexico's left-wing President Claudia Sheinbaum said in a post on X: "The people of Brazil won."Peru's right-wing President Keiko Fujimori praised Brazil's "democratic day". Similar messages were shared by the presidents of Chile and Ecuador.Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney noted that their two countries had already "flourished under our partnership".European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said "democracy and multilateralism" had won. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez - also a left-wing leader - called it a "great victory".French President Emmanuel Macron said the two nations should work "in service of a more just world".South African President Cyril Ramaphosa called Lula's victory one for the "global south and progressive forces throughout the world". Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Flávio Bolsonaro has refused to accept the result, calling for it to be annulledIn a video posted on Instagram later on Monday, Flávio Bolsonaro said police had told him to hand over his passports and had been banned from leaving the country. Trump has previously shown support for Bolsonaro's father Jair, who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence after being convicted of a coup attempt after losing the 2022 elections to Lula. Flávio Bolsonaro met Trump at the White House earlier this year to bid for his support.Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, has already been president for three non-consecutive terms, serving two terms between January 2003 to December 2010, and again from January 2023.His win makes him the first in Brazilian history to secure a fourth term, which will last until 2030.But this has been a bitterly fought campaign and the new term - set to start on 5 January - comes amid significant constraints at home and abroad, including animosity from the US president.Referring to what Trump has called the "Donroe Doctrine" -  which seeks to establish US dominance in the Western Hemisphere - Lula used his victory speech to insist that Brazil "will not accept being anyone's backyard".Lula has also bucked a wider trend in Latin America, where voters in countries such as Argentina, Chile and Colombia have put right-wing candidates and parties in power.

schema.headline: Brazil election: Lula wins fourth term in dramatic comeback over Bolsonaro

title: Algeria to send troops to Niger in first foreign deployment since 1973
description: Algeria is to send troops to Niger in its first foreign deployment since sending forces to Egypt during the Arab-Israeli war in 1973.The deployment fo
body: Algeria is to send troops to Niger in its first foreign deployment since sending forces to Egypt during the Arab-Israeli war in 1973.The deployment follows a visit to Algiers by Niger's defence minister, as the country seeks support against armed groups, some of which are linked to al-Qaeda or Islamic State.Algeria has economic interests in Niger, including a planned gas pipeline that would carry Nigerian gas through Niger to Algeria. The troops are expected to protect energy facilities in northern Niger, near the Libyan border.The deployment comes as the two neighbours rebuild ties after a diplomatic rift in 2025, when Niger recalled its ambassador to Algiers.Algeria's upper house of parliament held an emergency session on Sunday to vote on the proposed deployment. According to AFP news agency, 148 of the 174 senators voted in favour. It was later backed by the lower house of parliament.However, the timing and number of soldiers to be deployed have not been announced. The move would mark the first use of a 2020 constitutional provision allowing overseas military deployments and a significant shift in Algeria's long-standing policy against sending forces abroad."We are not sending our soldiers to wage war in Niger, but for a mission to secure economic infrastructure," Algerian senator Belkacem Boulghiti told reporters after the vote.Algeria's state-owned energy company, Sonatrach, has also signed an agreement with Niger's petroleum ministry to explore for oil in the Kafra region. Two exploration wells are estimated to contain 168 million and 100 million barrels, respectively, Reuters reported.Relations between Algeria and Niger have not always been smooth in recent years. Algeria condemned the 2023 coup that ousted Niger's elected President, Mohamed Bazoum, and brought Gen Abdourahamane Tchiani to power.Tensions rose again in 2025 after Algeria shot down a Malian drone near its border. Niger recalled its ambassador to Algiers in solidarity with Mali, a close ally which is also under military rule.Relations have since improved. Tchiani visited Algeria in February 2026, and in late August, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune sent fighter jets to Niger to help suppress a coup attempt and also donated four military helicopters.

schema.headline: Algeria to send troops to Niger in first foreign deployment since 1973

title: María Machado returns from exile to a Venezuela reshaped by Trump
description: Figure caption, Watch: Crowds welcome Venezuela's María Corina Machado after months in exileByWill GrantBBC's Mexico, Central America and Cuba corresp
body: Figure caption, Watch: Crowds welcome Venezuela's María Corina Machado after months in exileByWill GrantBBC's Mexico, Central America and Cuba correspondentDriving down roads lined with jubilant supporters from the western state of Lara to the capital Caracas, Maria Corina Machado's return to Venezuela could hardly have been more different to her exit 10 months earlier.Colourful, loud, open and defiant, it stood in stark contrast to the way the Venezuelan opposition leader slipped out of the country in the dead of night in December last year to receive the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo.She had been unable to make it back to her homeland until now, thwarted on several occasions by the Venezuelan government - and by the Trump administration,  which insisted the "time wasn't right" for her return.Now, it appears, it is."Maria Corina is the indisputable leader of Venezuela," says 20-year-old Gregory Noriega, wearing a sweatshirt emblazoned with the logo of the opposition movement Vente Venezuela. "Her return represents hope."Image caption, Gregory Noriega"This is a step forward in the electoral process which we've been waiting for since last year," echoes 18-year-old Hilary, who turned out on to the streets of the capital hoping to catch a glimpse of the opposition leader on her victory lap."She's returned after the double earthquakes when Venezuela needs her," adds her friend, Manuel.  "The whole country is behind her to show that now Venezuela isn't scared." Much has changed since Machado left Venezuelan soil to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. Then-President Nicolás Maduro is no longer at the top of the Venezuelan government.  Maduro was forcibly removed from power by US troops on 3 January, and whisked to New York where he faces drugs, weapons and torture charges – to which he's pleaded not guilty. He was replaced by his former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who has turned the page with Washington in ways few could have imagined. The bilateral relationship is today unrecognisable from the years of mutual animosity during the reigns of  President Hugo Chávez and then his handpicked successor, Maduro. The new circumstances throw up some interesting conundrums for both sides. When Machado left Venezuela, she had long been considered Washington's favoured alternative to Maduro. She returns to find the Trump administration perfectly happy with the one they've got – at least for the time being.Image source, Getty ImagesThe Trump administration recently signed a major oil deal with Venezuela which gave the US a 100-year concession over a staggering 65bn barrels of Venezuelan crude oil. The deal was reached in conjunction with a Venezuelan private company called North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) run by a businessman with a chequered past, Alejandro Betancourt.Machado has openly criticised the deal which the Rodríguez government reached with the US, albeit careful to direct her criticism at Caracas and at Betancourt rather than President Trump, to whom she gave her peace prize and whose trust and support she craves to move forward.President Trump has repeatedly said how satisfied he is with Delcy Rodríguez, calling her "wonderful" and "a terrific person". This was the vice-president of an administration he previously described as made up of "narco-communists".But the outpouring of jubilation for Machado's caravan into the capital shows she can still count on significant support on the streets, says Venezuelan political analyst Beningno Alarcon."The return of Maria Corina Machado, in my personal view, is the most significant [political] event since 3rd January," says Alarcon. "It means the most important political leader in Venezuela is back in the country.""The reception for her return shows that her ability to mobilise her support remains intact, which means the opposition in Venezuela now has something very solid: a leadership which is present on the ground as opposed to solely in exile," he says.Alarcon provides some evidence that the opposition – and the public at large – feel more emboldened since 3 January, a situation he believes will become only more pronounced with Machado's reappearance.Image caption, Political analyst Beningno AlarconFor instance, a joint study by the political think tanks Polis and Nexo suggests that Venezuela saw three times as many street protests in the first nine months of this year as in all of 2025, with demonstrations spanning a range of issues, from politics and working conditions to water supply.Furthermore, there's evidence that the repression of such protests has reduced by more than half.In such an environment, the return of a figurehead like Machado can galvanise an electorate that has spent years fearful of the consequences of speaking out.Her return also needs to be seen within the context of the wider talks brokered by Washington between the Venezuelan government and the opposition towards a negotiated political solution. Certainly, the US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, was quick to say her "safe return" to Venezuela was "the direct result of the US-supported reconciliation talks".The Nobel Peace Prize winner still faces charges in Venezuela ranging from treason to conspiracy of insurrection. For years, she and her supporters have dismissed the charges as politically motivated and baseless.Image caption, Young supporters of Maria MachadoHaving made at least eight attempts to return to Venezuela by air and by sea before the Trump administration gave her the green light, Machado now knows she has  Trump's blessing to be back on home soil – a position Delcy Rodríguez is both unwilling and unlikely to challenge.She called Machado's return a "show" and the entire cross-country event, which was livestreamed by her supporters over the weekend, was studiously ignored by state television outlets.But Rodríguez, too, needs a harmonious relationship with Washington if she is to avoid a fate similar to that of her predecessor and indicated she might be prepared to hold talks with Machado.For as much as Trump has complimented Rodríguez, he has also made it clear that Washington expects nothing less than her full submission and malleability on key issues like energy. Some reports have even suggested all major decision-making in the oil-rich nation is being largely dictated by Secretary Rubio via regular WhatsApp calls to the interim president.The young supporters gathered in droves in Caracas to cheer Maria Corina Machado home say their fears of criticising their government or demanding change are vanishing. Her return marked an irreversible political transition in Venezuela, they insist, one which they could barely fathom when she left for Oslo just a year ago.Figure caption, Watch:  December 2025 - BBC interview Nobel Peace Prize winner María Corina MachadoAdditional reporting by Vanessa Silva in Caracas.

schema.headline: María Machado returns from exile to a Venezuela reshaped by Trump

title: Serbia's veteran ruler Vučić concedes election to student-led protest movement
description: Celebrations in Serbia after veteran ruler Vučić loses election to student-led protest movementFigure caption, Watch: Joy and disbelief on Serbian str
body: Celebrations in Serbia after veteran ruler Vučić loses election to student-led protest movementFigure caption, Watch: Joy and disbelief on Serbian streets as Vučić concedes election defeatByAndré Rhoden-PaulJaroslav Lukiv and Paul KirbyEurope digital editorUpdated 26 October 2026Serbia's long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić has admitted defeat to a student-led protest movement in snap parliamentary elections.Celebrations erupted as crowds descended on the centre of Belgrade, Novi Sad and other cities. The student movement was formed less than two years ago in response to a railway station disaster blamed on corruption and negligence, but fought the election with candidates from a cross-section of Serbian society."It is clear we have lost these elections," right-wing populist leader Vučić said as he conceded. With 97% of polling stations counted, Serbia's election commission said the students had won 2.25 million votes and the former ruling party 1.67 million.The students had secured 52.7% of the vote, while Vučić's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) was on 39.2%, according to its preliminary figures late on Monday morning.Vučić had spent two terms as president and could not seek a third term, so was leading his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.He called the snap elections after two years of protests triggered by the collapse of a canopy in front of Novi Sad station which killed 16 people.Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, Vučić said early results made it "clear" that his party had lostThe Student List's lead candidate Ilija Srdanović told BBC Serbian: "This will be a free state."He said the anti-corruption movement, which had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia, hoped to "free the country from tyranny".There were celebrations on the streets of the city, with people dancing and chanting "victory", cars honking, and fireworks set off.  "Serbia is free," one student told the BBC. "It's a miracle."During a celebration speech, Student List candidate Radomir Saicic said Serbians  had shown "no obstacle was greater than their will", Reuters reported. "No force can forever overpower a people who have decided to take their destiny into their own hands," he added.Amid scenes of people dancing in the streets Belgrade, Selena Lebovic said the result was "really fabulous"."We are all crying, and what to say. We couldn't believe that it would be so easy," she told Reuters.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, An aerial photo shows the size of the celebrations by Students' List supporters at  Slavija square in BelgradeVučić made his announcement at the headquarters of his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in the capital Belgrade.The centre of Novi Sad - the northern city that triggered the student-led protests - was crowded. "Everything is going to get better now," David Vasić, one of those celebrating, told BBC Serbian.The Student List - which has no obvious leaders and whose members are not used to politics - had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia.It decided to field candidates to the 250-member parliament from across Serbian society including doctors, actors, academics and sports personalities."This is not an ordinary election victory, this is an avalanche that has wiped out an authoritarian regime and entire political scene," said Nebojša Vladisavljević, professor of political science at the University of Belgrade.There were now two big political groups in Serbia, and the Student List had "absolute legitimacy" to govern for the coming years, he told BBC Serbian.The anti-corruption movement campaigned on a manifesto that included purging officials who broke rules cracking down on protesters, stopping party loyalists from leading public enterprises, and freeing the public broadcaster of political control.Vučić and the SNS party have repeatedly denied corruption.Vučić, who backed Serbia's candidacy for the European Union while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, had pledged to increase pensions and public sector salaries, and investment in state healthcare.Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov praised Vučić's contribution to relations with Russia and hoped "the new political force" in Belgrade would understand that co-operation with Moscow was in Serbia's interests: "But, as you know, it takes two to tango."His defeat was welcomed by Hungary's prime minister, Péter Magyar, who said he was delighted to hear from the Student List's leaders "how much strength our victory in April had given them". Magyar's party ended 16 years of Viktor Orbán rule, while Vučić's SNS party had been in power since 2012.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Ilija Srdanović, Student List's leading candidate, pictured during celebrations late on SundayEuropean Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos said "a new chapter can begin for Serbia. The door to the EU is open, and we are ready to move forward together".Earlier in the day, long queues were seen outside polling stations in cities and towns across Serbia.This was also the case outside booths in a number of countries with sizeable Serbian communities - including Slovenia's capital Ljubljana, Germany's Munich, and Los Angeles and Chicago in the US.In France, Serbian voters waited in line in heavy rain in Paris.The election was held amid high tensions across Serbia, with police sealing off streets around the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK) in Belgrade.Attention will now turn to who will lead the Student List as prime minister. Presidential elections are due to take place in December, with parliament speaker Ana Brnabić currently filling the role in a caretaker capacity.

schema.headline: Serbia's veteran ruler Vučić concedes election to student-led protest movement

title: China's big political meeting could see Xi 'tighten discipline' in party
description: Past plenum sessions have been used to declare Xi as "the core" of the Party, abolish term limits which cleared the way for him to remain in power ind
body: Past plenum sessions have been used to declare Xi as "the core" of the Party, abolish term limits which cleared the way for him to remain in power indefinitely, and elevate his personal philosophy – branded as "Xi Jinping Thought" – to the same level as Chairman Mao.This year's plenum is an opportunity for Xi to dictate strategy in the run up to the Congress, ensuring that views are aligned and delegates loyal.Even the location of the meeting, which will wrap up on Thursday, has not been announced. Past plenums have been held inside Beijing's Jingxi Hotel.According to a readout from the powerful 21-member Politburo this September,  the plenum will adopt a decision on "several major issues persistently advancing the comprehensive strict governance of the Party", which is being read as a way to further ensure obedience and effectiveness from distant party officials.This means it would also be a time of nervousness for delegates as they look around the room with its "empty chairs" following the scale of recent purges within the Party.Allegations of corruption, even "moral corruption", have seen large swathes of senior figures culled."Moral corruption" has been seen by experts as a way of cracking down on perceived disloyalty to Xi because overall disloyalty to the Party can be interpreted as a breach of "morality".The Asia Society Policy Institute has estimated that of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022 only two have not been taken down.The all-powerful seven-man Central Military Commission, which runs the armed forces in China, has also been whittled down to only two people, Xi Jinping and one other general.This plenum is an opportunity for him to appoint new officers to this body.

schema.headline: China's big political meeting could see Xi 'tighten discipline' in party

title: Brazil election: How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp channel helped turn race around
description: The emergence of Lula's Army convinced many supporters that Brazil's left had finally found a way to compete in a digital arena. The shift was particu
body: The emergence of Lula's Army convinced many supporters that Brazil's left had finally found a way to compete in a digital arena. The shift was particularly significant because social media has played a central role in Brazilian politics since Jair Bolsonaro's 2018 election victory, when WhatsApp networks became a defining feature of political campaigning.Lula's Army messages often included ready-made templates for followers to share with friends and family. Each one assigned supporters a specific task aimed at boosting Lula's visibility on social media.Janones frequently instructed his "troops" to "blow up" the latest campaign video or help a new hashtag "take off"."Guys, urgent!", "Don't go to sleep yet", "No food before the mission!", and "I have one more task before you're dismissed", were some of the instructions.On the eve of the election, the congressman also hosted a 24-hour live event - dubbed the "turnaround livestream" - even as polls continued to suggest a victory for Bolsonaro.The tactic worked, despite worries by some members of the Workers' Party that Janones's often-confrontational style on social media could undermine the more moderate image they hoped to project for Lula.In his victory speech, Lula referred to Janones as "our General" and thanked him for "raising the morale of our troops every day".Measuring the electoral impact of online mobilisation, however, is notoriously difficult. While Lula's allies credit Lula's Army with helping fuel the comeback, political scientists caution that it is impossible to determine how many votes, if any, were directly influenced by the WhatsApp operation.Political scientist Denilde Holzhacker argues that a shift in Lula's campaign strategy was key to his comeback. Rather than relying solely on online engagement, she says the Workers' Party candidate succeeded in connecting digital campaigning with grassroots mobilisation on the ground.According to Holzhacker, the campaign intensified local efforts and adapted its messaging - linking a Bolsonaro victory with concerns about potential changes to social programmes and the loss of rights."It was to Lula's credit that he recognised his own weakness and completely changed his style," she says. "And Janones managed to do something that had seemed unthinkable for Brazil's left - dominate social media."By contrast, Holzhacker argues that Flávio Bolsonaro entered the run-off overly confident of victory and failed to communicate his message to his supporters as effectively.Sociologist and political scientist Mayra Goulart, a professor at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, also cautions against attributing Lula's comeback solely to social media."It was a combination of social media and street-level mobilisation," she says. "The physical world enabled a form of mobilisation capable of reducing abstention and persuading undecided voters."In her view, Lula's supporters succeeded in turning online enthusiasm into real-world political engagement."Those committed to Lula's victory worked to bring people together and persuade them to vote," Goulart says.She argues that the effort not only helped increase turnout but could also prove valuable for Lula's next administration."I believe this collective effort was an important learning experience and will prove valuable for a government that still faces many battles ahead. It not only helped reduce abstention, but also converted a significant number of undecided voters."Lula himself suggested that the mobilisation behind his comeback could shape the way he governs in the years ahead.In his victory speech, he said the election had taught him many lessons and pledged to change the way Brazil is governed."We are going to give people a greater say in decision-making, and digital communication will play a much bigger role in my government."

schema.headline: Brazil election: How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp channel helped turn race around

title: Chris Brown: US singer given suspended eight-month prison sentence over nightclub attack
description: US singer Chris Brown has avoided jail after striking a man twice in the head with a glass tequila bottle in a London nightclub.The R&B star was given
body: US singer Chris Brown has avoided jail after striking a man twice in the head with a glass tequila bottle in a London nightclub.The R&B star was given an eight-month prison sentence, suspended for 12 months, over the attack at private members' club Tape in Mayfair, in the early hours of 19 February 2023.Brown's vocal coach, rapper Omololu Akinlolu, who joined the attack, was sentenced to four months' imprisonment, suspended for 12 months. Both men, who had pleaded guilty to affray, were also ordered to pay £1,500 costs.Judge Tony Baumgartner said Brown's use of the glass bottle to hit the victim twice over the head "was plainly dangerous", adding that the violence of the attack was "intense".The sentence means Brown will not be imprisoned unless he commits another offence during the 12-month period of suspension. The court heard Brown's attack on music producer Abraham 'Abe' Diaw left the victim in need of hospital treatment for his injuries. In sentencing, Judge Baumgartner said: "The repeated use of a glass bottle in that way, especially aimed at the head, was plainly dangerous, it carried the risk of delivering a more serious injury than was ultimately sustained."CCTV footage was shown where Brown struck Diaw four times with the bottle, connecting twice with his head, and then hitting his shoulder.Sentencing Brown, Judge Baumgartner said: "This was not planned violence. It was nevertheless serious violence by two people in a crowded nightclub."The judge told Brown: "Violence of this kind in a crowded nightclub is serious, it creates an obvious risk, not only to the person against whom it is directed, but also to others nearby."He added that Brown's conduct was "particularly dangerous" and that he had to be "physically pulled away" from the attack.The judge said Brown's fame, commercial success and professional standing "do not entitle you to special treatment - the law applies equally to everyone". But judge Baumgartner also said he had noted Brown's guilty plea, compliance with bail conditions, and the impact a custodial sentence would have on Brown's children, and said the singer's "risk of further offending is low".Brown and Akinlolu pleaded guilty to a charge of affray at Southwark Crown Court in July. The singer had been due to face a trial on more serious charges, which he denied, and which were subsequently dropped.These were assault, attempting to cause grievous bodily harm, and having an offensive weapon.Following Brown and Akinlolu's guilty pleas, the CPS released a statement outlining that Brown had approached Diaw on the dance floor, hitting him over the head with a glass bottle twice, before Akinlolu then punched Diaw in the head."They continued their assault whilst the victim attempted to flee through the club," the CPS said. "The victim was kicked while he was seated defenceless on the floor."Judge Baumgartner told the pair that while he had concluded they had both crossed the threshold to be jailed, this year's changes to sentencing laws meant that he had to put off doing so, unless there were exceptional reasons."I have considered whether the seriousness of the offending, taken together with the need for punishment and deterrence, amounts to exceptional circumstances requiring immediate imprisonment. I have concluded, in relation to each of you, that it does not," he said."These were serious offences deserving of custodial sentences, but the circumstances do not justify displacing the [new legal] requirement that those sentences be suspended."On Monday, the court was shown three pieces of CCTV footage from inside Tape nightclub on the night of the attack.The attack lasted no more than 20 seconds, but Brown could be seen hitting the victim four times with a tequila bottle, twice to the head.Prosecutor, Heidi Stonecliffe KC, described the weapon as a "heavy square-shaped tequila bottle" and said Diaw was approached by Brown at around 03:00.The footage showed that the nightclub was very small and packed at the time.The defence described Chris Brown as a "dedicated and a loving father of four children," someone who is "positive and present".The singer is described as having lived "a good and law-abiding life" since his last conviction in 2013.The events in Tape nightclub were described by the defence as a "short and deeply regretted incident".Brown's defence lawyer told the court that he apologises to all those present at the club at the time of the attack."This is an ugly and unattractive incident," Sallie Bennett-Jenkins KC said."It is, however, an incident which was very short-lived, lasting something more than 17 seconds but no more than 20."It is something which undoubtedly would have caused distress to those who are present and for which Mr Brown... offers a profound apology to all those present."The court heard Akinlolu "genuinely believed" that Brown was "under attack" when he joined the attack, punching Diaw.Brown was described as being like a "brother" to Akinlolu, his lawyer Laurie-Anne Power KC told the court.She added: "He genuinely believed him to be under attack and became involved, and thereafter accepts his initial involvement very quickly evolved into the events he has pleaded guilty to."Diaw was taken to St Mary's Hospital in London after the attack. Ms Stonecliffe KC said he was discharged with "pain relief and a diagnosis of head injury and superficial injury of the knee".An MRI scan taken in early March showed a "high grade injury to a ligament on the inner side of the left knee", the court heard.Defending Brown, Ms Bennett-Jenkins KC said there was a "relatively low level of force" and disputed how significant the injuries were.The defence argued that the attack left no fractures or broken skin and there was an absence of serious injuries.Diaw, the victim, was "not supportive of the prosecution" and "withdrew" his support some time after the incident, the court heard.Brown and Akinlolu stood up and faced one another and clasped hands after the judge concluded his sentencing remarks before walking out of the glass dock.There were loud cheers outside the court as Chris Brown left the building as he appeared to stop to sign an autograph.After the sentencing, Brown shared a video from inside his car on his Instagram story, showing him looking out the window before turning to the camera and giving a thumbs-up.Affray is an offence under the Public Order Act and a person is deemed guilty in law if they use or threaten "unlawful violence towards another" with their behaviour, leading someone to fear for their personal safety.Brown, 37, is considered one of the biggest stars in R&B, with a string of hit songs including Turn Up The Music, Ayo, Freaky Friday, Run It, Forever, Yeah 3x and Don't Wake Me Up.

schema.headline: Chris Brown: US singer given suspended eight-month prison sentence over nightclub attack

title: Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again
description: Lula's first presidential victory in 2002 marked the end of an unprecedented journey from poverty.The son of a poor, illiterate peasant family, Lula w
body: Lula's first presidential victory in 2002 marked the end of an unprecedented journey from poverty.The son of a poor, illiterate peasant family, Lula worked as a peanut seller and shoe-shine boy as a child, only learning to read when he was 10 years old.He went on to train as a metalworker and found work in an industrial city near São Paulo, where he lost the little finger of his left hand in an accident in the 1960s.Lula was not initially interested in politics, but threw himself into trade union activism.Elected leader of the 100,000-strong Metalworkers' Union in 1975, he transformed trade union activism in Brazil by turning what had mostly been government-friendly organisations into a powerful independent movement.In 1980, Lula brought together a combination of trade unionists, intellectuals, Trotskyites and Church activists to found the Workers' Party (PT), the first major socialist party in the country's history.The PT went on to gradually replace its revolutionary commitment to changing the power structure in Brazil with a more pragmatic, social democratic platform.Lula came to power promising major reforms to the country's political and economic system.He vowed to eradicate hunger and create a self-confident, caring, outward-looking nation.In his time in office, Lula pumped billions of dollars into social programmes and can reasonably claim to have helped reverse Brazil's historic inequalities.By increasing the minimum wage well above the rate of inflation and broadening state help to the most impoverished with a family grant programme, the Bolsa Familia, he helped some 44 million people and cemented his support among the poor.However, many commentators argue that the programme failed to address the structural problems that underpin poverty, such as a lack of education.He left office eight years later, after serving two terms as president, enjoying exceptionally high popularity ratings for a retiring Latin American leader - 83% - having raised Brazil's profile on the international scene and presided over the longest period of economic growth in three decades.Unable to run for a third term, Lula left the presidency and, shortly afterwards, was diagnosed with throat cancer. He even shaved his trademark beard during treatment. Doctors declared him cured of the disease in 2012.Under his chosen successor, progress stalled. The economic boom also gave way to recession, and the country's political scene was rocked by a huge investigation into top-level corruption, known as Operation Car Wash.Lula was among those to get caught up in the scandal. In July 2017, he was convicted of corruption and sentenced to more than nine years in prison for accepting a beachside flat as a bribe from engineering firm OAS - a sentence increased on appeal to 12 years.Lula was also jailed for 12 years and 11 months for corruption and money laundering for receiving bribes from two construction and engineering firms by way of funding improvements in a country house he and his family used.He has always maintained his innocence, insisting accusations against him were politically motivated. In 2019, he was released after having served just over 18 months, after a Supreme Court ruling that the incarceration had been illegal, having come before all appeals had been exhausted.Those convictions were annulled in 2021, leaving Lula free to run for a third term in 2022, beating right-winger Jair Bolsonaro.When he re-entered office in 2023, he vowed it would be his last term, and yet his party endorsed him as their candidate again this year, even though he will turn 81 on Tuesday. Even backers of the PT will acknowledge that he achieved more in his first two terms - from January 2003 to December 2010 - than in his most recent four years in office. And while his supporters described him ahead of the 2022 election as the "saviour of the Amazon", praising his commitment to protecting the rainforest, some environmentalists have been critical of some of his recent actions. His support for exploratory oil drilling in offshore waters near the mouth of the Amazon in particular has drawn criticism. Lula insists that he remains committed to eventually phasing out fossil fuels and argues that oil revenues are key to financing Brazil's transition to clean energy. His government has also pointed to the reduction in deforestation in the Amazon - satellite data suggests the area deforested in the first half of 2026 was reduced to its lowest in the past decade - as proof that its policies were working.  Lula's third term coincided with the return to office of Trump.The two men represent different ends of the political spectrum and have found it impossible not to voice their differences in public.The Brazilian leader told the BBC in September 2025 that he had no relationship with Trump.Even though the US has a trade surplus with Brazil, Donald Trump imposed 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods in July that year, citing the trial on coup charges of Brazil's right-wing former president Jair Bolsonaro as a trigger. Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year jail sentence and it was his son, Flávio, who Lula beat in Sunday's election run-off.Lula accused Trump of foreign interference and said "he's not emperor of the world". But their relationship improved after a White House in May this year, after which the two leaders exchanged public compliments - Trump called Lula "dynamic", while the Brazilian president said he left the meeting "very satisfied".In July of this year, the US imposed 25% tariffs on most goods, external from Brazil.The two governments still disagree on key issues such as crime, and Lula acknowledged they are especially far apart on trade.Referring to what Trump has dubbed the "Donroe doctrine" - his administration's national security strategy which asserts that US dominance in the Western hemisphere should not be interfered with - Lula has insisted that "Brazil does not fit into anyone's backyard".

schema.headline: Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again

title: Ballon d'Or predictions: Will Lamine Yamal, Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe or Lionel Messi win?
description: European football expert Julien Laurens: I think he was the best player in Europe last season, especially in the Champions League where he was outstan
body: European football expert Julien Laurens: I think he was the best player in Europe last season, especially in the Champions League where he was outstanding. He helped lead the team to another title, a back-to-back one. He got the penalty in the final, scored in both semi-finals, in the quarter-final, and in the last 16. He was amazing in those huge, huge games where you want your best players to step up. He deserves to win the Ballon d'Or for being the best player in the world all the way up to the World Cup. He won't win it, unfortunately, because Lamine Yamal, for the player he is and how entertaining and spectacular he is, didn't really shine at the World Cup, even if Spain won it. He didn't really do that well in the Champions League for Barcelona, getting knocked out early. However, his style of football means he'll probably win it - but it should be Kvaratskhelia.Ex-Liverpool and Blackburn full-back Stephen Warnock: I think it will be Lamine Yamal for helping Spain to win the World Cup. If you were asking who else is in the hunt, I would say Michael Olise, but my pick personally would be Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, he is unbelievable. I love watching him play. He had such an impact for Paris St-Germain and last season he was incredible. I just don't think he will get the votes with Georgia not being in the World Cup.BBC Radio 5 Live Euro Leagues guest and Athletic reporter Rory Smith: It will probably go to Lamine Yamal because it generally goes to someone who has won the biggest trophy, and this is the World Cup. It shouldn't be him because he wasn't necessarily Spain's most important player but his fame and talent means it will be him. Personally I would give it to Kvaratskhelia. He has been the most exciting player in European club football for a while now, a valuable part of the PSG team who retained the Champions League, and crucially I think you shouldn't suffer because you come from a country who isn't in the running to win the World Cup.

schema.headline: Ballon d'Or predictions: Will Lamine Yamal, Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe or Lionel Messi win?

title: Catholic bishops apologise for 'exploited' Trump meeting
description: Two Catholic bishops in the US have said they regret meeting President Donald Trump at the White House, after images of them praying with him were rel
body: Two Catholic bishops in the US have said they regret meeting President Donald Trump at the White House, after images of them praying with him were released and prompted many to ask if they were making a political statement.Photos and video of the 22 October meeting show a group of bishops standing around Trump at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office.Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey Grob, one of those pictured, said he had believed the meeting was private and not "a political photo opportunity".Trump and Pope Leo XIV have a contentious relationship, and some US bishops have criticised the White House's immigration stance. Trump won the support of 55% of Catholic voters in 2024, a Pew study found.In a statement posted online, Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines, Iowa, said the meeting was arranged by officials with the White House Faith Office to discuss issues including immigration, visas for international clergy and the "exploitation of vulnerable poor persons". "In no way did any of us intend by our involvement to endorse any political party or any individual candidate," Joensen said. "I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes," he added.A video of the meeting was released by Margo Martin, a special assistant to the president and communications adviser who frequently shares behind-the-scenes images of Trump on social media. Archbishop Grob said that after 90 minutes of meetings with officials, the religious leaders were ushered into the Oval Office to pray with Trump. Grob said images of the meeting later caused concern among some of his congregants. "I soon began receiving messages of serious concern over the possibility that I had inadvertently participated in a political event less than two weeks before a national election," he wrote."I also heard from some who felt wounded because of the ways they or their family have been harmed by the president's policies," he added. Grob said none of the participants in the meeting gave permission for the public distribution or posting of video or photos of the event. When contacted for comment by the BBC, the White House did not directly address questions regarding the meeting or subsequent comments by the two bishops. "There has never been a greater president for Catholic Americans than President Trump, and his strong record proves it," White House Spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement. According to Pew Research Center, which analyses religion in the US, opinions of Trump's performance have slipped among all major religious groups. In a survey this month, 30% of all US Catholics said they approved of his job performance, compared to 47% when he returned to the White House in 2025.That could have an effect on the 3 November midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress. More Catholics in the survey, 42%, said they preferred the Democrats running in their local House of Representatives races, where slightly less, 39% favoured Republicans.During his second term, Trump has had a tense relationship with the head of the Catholic church, Pope Leo, as he has moved aggressively to remove people believed to be in the US illegally.Nine days before the Oval Office meeting with the bishops took place, Bishop Brendon Cahill and Walter Kim, the president of the National Association of Evangelicals, issued a statement urging "Christian compassion and wisdom in the immigration debate".They said the immigration clampdown has led to the "sowing of fear, the fracturing of families, the deprivation of due process, and the vilification of our neighbors."The US Conference of Catholic Bishops also recently condemned the Trump administration's plans to livestream a military execution, which were later scrapped.Both Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are Catholics who have visited the Vatican during Trump's second term.A Midwestern member of the bishops' conference, Robert Barron of Minnesota, agreed to serve on the president's Religious Liberty Commission last year, as did former New York Archbishop Timothy Dolan.

schema.headline: Catholic bishops apologise for 'exploited' Trump meeting

title: Ethiopia attacks: More than 60 Orthodox Christians killed in Oromia
description: More than 60 people have been killed in a series of attacks on Christians in Ethiopia's Oromia region, according to the country's Orthodox Church.One
body: More than 60 people have been killed in a series of attacks on Christians in Ethiopia's Oromia region, according to the country's Orthodox Church.One resident, whose 75-year-old father was killed, described it as an ambush. "We were completely unprepared and had no prior knowledge. They surrounded us from all four directions," he told BBC Amharic.The regional government said that it would take action against those responsible.A local official blamed the attacks on a newly formed rebel coalition, the Alliance for Survival, which includes the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA). The OLA has not commented but has denied carrying out previous such attacks.A statement from the Holy Synod of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church said that 20 houses were burnt to the ground in the attacks. It did not say who was responsible.Eyewitness told BBC Amharic that five of those killed were children.A church official described the attacks on three areas in the Shirka district as a "massacre", saying security forces arrived at the scene but were unable to stop the assault.Many residents have now fled the area.Condemning the violence, the Orthodox Church said attacks against Christians had been increasing recently, and that "such actions undermine the country's values of mutual respect and peaceful coexistence".In a statement posted on Facebook, the Orthodox Church said it had repeatedly raised concerns about insecurity with authorities at different levels of government, but that "so far there has been no solution".The Ethiopian Human Rights Council, a non-governmental organisation, said in a report released in July 2026 that 458 people had been killed in attacks in that area over the previous four years.But this is one of the most deadly attacks in that period.The report said armed groups had repeatedly targeted local communities, particularly followers of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, in what it described as religiously motivated attacks.The government has previously blamed the OLA for the attacks, with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed saying violence targeting civilians and religious institutions was part of a plan to destabilise the country.The group, which says it is fighting for greater rights for the Oromo people, denies these allegations.Previous reports have also documented attacks against Muslims in the area. Residents who spoke to the BBC on various occasions have described the violence as both ethnic and religious in nature.About two-thirds of Ethiopians are Christians, mostly Orthodox, while one third are Muslim.

schema.headline: Ethiopia attacks: More than 60 Orthodox Christians killed in Oromia

title: Anthropic warns of AI's 'catastrophic risks' ahead of major IPO
description: Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blo
body: Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.The firm's valuation is expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which was the biggest-ever listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion in the summer.Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be released, their price range, or a date for the listing.The Claude chatbot developer reported $16.3bn (£12.2bn) of revenue in the first half of the year, with losses of more than $80.7bn. Anthropic, which said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".Anthropic was founded five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five others, and announced its intention to go public in June.Its main rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.Those announcements were followed by a wave of cyber-security and other technological breaches involving their AI agents - bots designed to operate somewhat autonomously.Current and former staff of both companies also warned AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.As Anthropic revealed its stock debut plans on Monday, the owners of the rights to Elvis Presley's music sued the AI firm accusing it of using hundreds of the rock-and-roll star's songs to train its chatbot Claude.In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.Anthropic detailed losses in its financial filings that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance"."In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said.Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business".Across about 90 pages detailing possible risk factors, Anthropic set out the potential threats to its ability to safely and competitively develop AI. Anthropic warned it relies on a cluster of cloud computing providers, Taiwanese chipmakers already facing huge demand and data centres concentrated in the US.It also warned of "regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models" - citing concerns over AI being used by children or individuals at risk of suicide - and uncertainty about where and how it might be held liable for actions taken by its systems.However, Anthropic also used the filing to laud the potential benefits of the tech itself, envisioning it unlocking "millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionise every area of human endeavour" across a range of fields."We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," the firm said.Anthropic said AI would also "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine", potentially finding cures to diseases including cancer and Alzheimer's.The firm added it could also establish "sustained acceleration in economic growth" by boosting productivity.

schema.headline: Anthropic warns of AI's 'catastrophic risks' ahead of major IPO

title: Ex-FBI chief James Comey faces federal charges for third time
description: Federal prosecutors have taken steps to charge ex-Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director James Comey with leaking national defence information
body: Federal prosecutors have taken steps to charge ex-Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director James Comey with leaking national defence information, according to a court filing. It marks the third time the justice department has moved to bring criminal charges against Comey, a longtime critic of President Donald Trump.Few details are provided about the two counts in the three-page filing, but Comey's lawyers said in separate court papers that the case stemmed from an alleged disclosure of classified information to the New York Times in October 2016, while he was head of the FBI.Comey denied any wrongdoing in a video posted on Substack on Monday, calling the charges an "appalling abuse"."It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the department of justice, one that we cannot become numb to," he said in the clip."Nothing's changed with me - I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary."Comey was charged in Washington DC through a criminal information, which is a formal written charging document filed directly by a prosecutor.This is different to a criminal indictment, which must be approved by a grand jury, a group of citizens sworn in to review if evidence is strong enough to prosecute.Comey's lawyer, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement that two different teams of prosecutors had investigated the alleged disclosure to the New York Times a decade ago during the first Trump administration. "Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone," he said. The attorney said the court filing "purports to charge Mr Comey with crimes that he did not commit".His legal team has filed a motion to dismiss the charges.Former federal prosecutor Glenn Kirschner told the BBC that the case may have exceeded the 10-year statute of limitations, giving the motion to dismiss the charges "a very good chance of being granted".Kirschner said it seemed like the charges against Comey were a "revenge-fuelled attempt by Donald Trump to have his Department of Justice find something that might stick".Comey was fired by Trump during his first term, after the former FBI director opened an investigation into claims of Russian meddling in the US 2016 presidential election.Since then, Trump has repeatedly called for his prosecution, and these charges are the administration's third attempt to do so.Comey was first indicted by a federal grand jury in September 2025 on charges that he had lied to Congress during testimony and obstructed a congressional proceeding.He pleaded not guilty the following month before the case was dismissed in November.In April 2026, Comey surrendered to authorities to face charges alleging that an image he briefly shared on social media posed a threat to Trump's life.The case stemmed from a 2025 Instagram post by Comey, which contained a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to read "86 47". "Eighty-six" is a slang term for "get rid of", and prosecutors allege it encourages violence against Trump, the 47th president.Comey denies any wrongdoing, saying he did not know what the numbers meant, and accusing the prosecution of political motivation. That case is ongoing.The latest charges against Comey were made public the same day a federal judge ruled the justice department illegally fired his daughter, Maurene Comey.Maurene Comey, who lost her job as a federal prosecutor in New York in July 2025, sued the government, arguing she was unlawfully fired because of her father and because of her perceived political affiliations.The judge ruled on Monday that the Trump administration must reinstate her and that she must be given back pay.

schema.headline: Ex-FBI chief James Comey faces federal charges for third time

title: Ebola outbreak: DR Congo nurse killed in attack as Uganda tightens border
description: A nurse has been killed and another health worker seriously injured in an attack as they were responding to an Ebola alert in north-eastern Democratic
body: A nurse has been killed and another health worker seriously injured in an attack as they were responding to an Ebola alert in north-eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.The two were targeted by local youths who accused them of contaminating water sources and spreading the Ebola virus, according to the UN-backed Radio Okapi. The World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the attack.In an attempt to prevent the virus spreading, neighbouring Uganda has banned all non-essential travel to and from DR Congo  and says its citizens returning from there will be quarantined for 21 days. More than 4,800 people have died and nearly 10,000 been infected in DR Congo since this outbreak began in May.Reacting to the attack in DR Congo, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said health workers "must be able to carry out their duties in safety and dignity", adding that healthcare personnel should always be protected.The UN agency also extended its condolences to the family and colleagues of the nurse who was killed and wished the injured worker a swift recovery.The BBC has contacted the Ebola response team for comment on the circumstances surrounding the attack in DR Congo.This is not the first time such an attack has happened in DR Congo. Last month, a politician was beaten to death after promoting measures to stop the spread of Ebola, while in August, the Red Cross said its volunteers had been injured and an ambulance set on fire in 11 violent incidents during the first 100 days after the outbreak was declared.Earlier this month, two countries - Kenya and Nigeria - reported their first cases of Ebola linked to the current outbreak. The patient in Nigeria was on Monday flown from Abuja to Switzerland for further treatment.She is the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat who had travelled to the Ugandan capital for a holiday, according to the head of Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention Jean Kaseya. She was evacuated alongside her husband, who has shown no symptoms.Nigeria's health ministry said she was stable, conscious and able to communicate.Authorities are now trying to establish where she contracted the virus.The new restrictions announced in Uganda come after questions were raised over her case and that of a Kenyan businessman. Both tested positive for Ebola after travelling through Uganda, even though no cases have been reported there since August. The Kenyan had arrived from DR Congo where he had business interests.Only essential travellers, including aid workers, truck drivers and security personnel, will be allowed to cross the border from DR Congo to Uganda, subject to strict health screening, the health ministry announced.In addition, all travellers entering Uganda, regardless of their country of origin, will be required to complete locator forms to facilitate contact tracing where necessary.It said returning Ugandans would "undergo 21 days of quarantine at their own cost".About 60 people who were being monitored after coming into contact with the Kenyan patient have all been discharged, it added. In Kenya, the first group of 20 contacts of the first case have gone home, after spending 21 days in quarantine, the health ministry announced on Monday.Another 98 are still being supervised, while seven people who have tested positive for Ebola were stable it said.The Kenyan businessman died two days after arriving in Nairobi. A second woman, related to the businessman, died over the weekend."All these are measures to ensure that we keep Uganda free of Ebola," Uganda's Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi told the BBC's Newsday programme. Since the two cases were reported in Kenya and Nigeria this month, Uganda has repeatedly stressed that no cases have been reported within its borders. Uganda recorded 20 Ebola cases and two people died shortly after the outbreak started in DR Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country free of the disease in August.The two passengers tested positive after passing through Uganda's Entebbe airport on the same day.Diana Atwine, the health ministry's permanent secretary, said CCTV camera footage showed no physical interaction between the two patients.Ugandan officials had previously said the patient in Nigeria had travelled to eastern DR Congo, only transiting through Uganda. On Sunday, however, the health ministry said Uganda and Nigeria were both working to establish her movements, complete travel history and possible routes of exposure.The Ugandan health minister said the recent cases meant the risk had not ended and further underscored the need to "remain vigilant"."We share a border with [DR Congo], where transmission continues, and our communities remain closely connected through trade, travel and family ties," Baryomunsi said.The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.The Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind this outbreak is relatively rare and there is still no vaccine or specific treatment - though trials are under way.Additional reporting by Swaibu Ibrahim in Kampala

schema.headline: Ebola outbreak: DR Congo nurse killed in attack as Uganda tightens border

title: Jordan says 'terrorists' killed in Syria in retaliatory strike over church attack
description: In response to the strike, Syria said it had closed a border crossing with Jordan."The decision includes the complete suspension of passenger and comm
body: In response to the strike, Syria said it had closed a border crossing with Jordan."The decision includes the complete suspension of passenger and commercial traffic in both directions, to ensure the safety of travellers and workers at the crossing," Syrian authorities said in a statement carried by state media.It added that it had "opened direct channels of communication" with Jordanian officials and had launched "comprehensive investigations to establish the full circumstances of the targeting".Nassib is the only passenger and commercial border crossing between Jordan and Syria.Earlier on Monday, senior government security officials said Jordanian security forces had arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law over the church attack. The Public Security Directorate (PSD) said the unnamed "terrorists" were found hiding in an abandoned house in Karak before dawn.Jordan's Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told state-affiliated TV the attackers were all Jordanians and "had been holed up in a building in one of the villages near the site of the attack".

schema.headline: Jordan says 'terrorists' killed in Syria in retaliatory strike over church attack
